claim: The purple sea urchin genome encodes 10 IL17 subfamilies (35 genes) and 2 IL17 receptors.
source: The purple sea urchin genome encodes 10 IL17 subfamilies (35 genes) and 2 IL17 receptors.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by genomic analysis presented in the Results section, including phylogenetic trees and gene identification methods.

claim: Two IL17 subfamilies are sequentially strongly upregulated and attenuated in the gut epithelium in response to bacterial disturbance.
source: Two IL17 subfamilies are sequentially strongly upregulated and attenuated in the gut epithelium in response to bacterial disturbance.
evidence: Supported by RNA-Seq data, RT-qPCR measurements, and in situ hybridization showing temporal expression patterns of SpIL17-1 and SpIL17-4 genes.

claim: IL17R1 signal perturbation results in reduced expression of several response genes including an IL17 subtype.
source: IL17R1 signal perturbation results in reduced expression of several response genes including an IL17 subtype, indicating a potential feedback.
evidence: Demonstrated through MASO experiments showing reduced expression of SpIL17-4 and other immune genes when IL17R1 is perturbed.

claim: A third IL17 subfamily is activated in adult immune cells.
source: A third IL17 subfamily is activated in adult immune cells indicating that expression in immune cells and epithelia is divided among families.
evidence: Shown by RT-qPCR analysis of SpIL17-9 expression in adult coelomocytes following immune challenge.

claim: Most of the IL17 subfamilies are conserved throughout echinoderms.
source: Most of these subfamilies are conserved throughout echinoderms.
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analysis of IL17 sequences from multiple echinoderm species showing conservation of subfamilies.

claim: IL17 cytokines are central mediators of mammalian immunity.
source: IL17 cytokines are central mediators of mammalian immunity.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about IL17 function in mammals.

claim: Sea urchins share a molecular heritage with chordates that includes the IL17 system.
source: Sea urchins share a molecular heritage with chordates that includes the IL17 system.
evidence: Based on phylogenetic relationships and the presence of IL17 genes in both sea urchins and chordates as deuterostomes.

claim: The difficulty in identifying homologs of mammalian cytokines remains a long-standing barrier to comparative immunology approaches.
source: The difficulty in identifying homologs of mammalian cytokines, even within other vertebrate classes (Secombes et al., 2011), remains a long-standing barrier to this approach.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work discussing challenges in cytokine identification.

claim: Cytokines are subject to high levels of evolutionary pressure and sequence diversification.
source: As central mediators of the immune response, cytokines are key targets for pathogen mimicry or co-option (Elde and Malik, 2009; Epperson et al., 2012) and are subject to high levels of evolutionary pressure and sequence diversification (Koyanagi et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on pathogen interactions with cytokines and evolutionary diversification.

claim: IL17 cytokines are characterized by a cysteine-knot fold structure formed through interactions among four conserved cysteine residues.
source: These proteins are characterized by a cysteine-knot fold structure that is formed through interactions among four conserved cysteine residues (Hymowitz et al., 2001).
evidence: This structural feature is established in the literature and cited from structural studies.

claim: IL17 cytokines have been functionally characterized in jawed and jawless vertebrates.
source: IL17 cytokines have been functionally characterized in jawed (Kolls and Lindén, 2004) and jawless vertebrates (Smith et al., 2013; Han et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citations to functional studies in different vertebrate groups.

claim: IL17 orthologs have been identified in invertebrate deuterostomes, molluscs, nematodes and arthropods (Daphnia).
source: orthologs have been identified also in invertebrate deuterostomes (Huang et al., 2008; Hibino et al., 2006) molluscs, nematodes and arthropods (Daphnia) (Huang et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies identifying IL17 in various invertebrate taxa.

claim: IL17 factors are absent from available genome sequences of insects and non-bilaterian metazoans.
source: In contrast, IL17 factors are absent from available genome sequences of insects and non-bilaterian metazoans.
evidence: This is an inference based on genomic surveys and absence of IL17 sequences in these taxa.

claim: Most mammalian genomes encode six IL17 family members (IL17A-F).
source: Most mammalian genomes encode six IL17 family members (IL17A-F) (Kolls and Lindén, 2004)
evidence: This is established knowledge about mammalian IL17 genes supported by citation.

claim: IL17A and IL17F define subsets of effector T cells (Th17 cells and γδ17 cells) and innate lymphocyte-like cells (ILCs) and induce strong inflammatory responses.
source: These two highly expressed cytokines define subsets of effector T cells (Th17 cells and γδ17 cells) and innate lymphocyte-like cells (ILCs) and induce strong inflammatory responses (Korn et al., 2009; Lockhart et al., 2006; Gladiator et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to studies on IL17-producing cell types and their functions.

claim: Three members of the IL17 family (IL17B, IL17C, and IL17E) are expressed by epithelial cells, including those in the gut.
source: Importantly, IL17 expression is not restricted to lymphocytes or other mesodermal immune cells. Three members of the IL17 family (IL17B, IL17C, and IL17E [also known as IL-25]) are expressed by epithelial cells, including those in the gut (Song et al., 2011; Ramirez-Carrozzi et al., 2011; Reynolds et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies demonstrating epithelial expression of these IL17 family members.

claim: IL17C is a key factor in the early intestinal immune response where it regulates the expression of many innate immune genes.
source: In this context, IL17C is a key factor in the early intestinal immune response where it regulates the expression of many innate immune genes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about IL17C function in mammalian gut immunity.

claim: In colonic epithelial cells, IL17E promotes inflammation through the IL17RB receptor, while IL17B competitively binds with IL17RB to interfere with this signal.
source: In colonic epithelial cells, IL17E promotes inflammation through the IL17RB receptor, while IL17B competitively binds with IL17RB to interfere with this signal (Reynolds et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to a study on IL17E and IL17B receptor interactions.

claim: The purple sea urchin genome sequence encodes an expansive set of immune receptors and effectors as well as conserved signaling pathways.
source: The purple sea urchin genome sequence encodes an expansive set of immune receptors and effectors as well as conserved signaling pathways downstream of pattern recognition receptors and homologs of a suite of transcription factors that have key roles in modulating the immune response and hematopoiesis in vertebrates (Hibino et al., 2006; Sodergren et al., 2006; Rast et al., 2006; Messier-Solek et al., 2010; Buckley and Rast, 2012, 2015; Solek et al., 2013; Schrankel et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to genomic and functional studies of sea urchin immunity.

claim: Purple sea urchins undergo indirect development with a bilaterally symmetric, planktonic larval form that metamorphoses into a pentameral adult.
source: Purple sea urchins undergo indirect development with a bilaterally symmetric, planktonic larval form that metamorphoses into a pentameral adult.
evidence: This is established knowledge about sea urchin development supported by citation.

claim: At 10 days post-fertilization, larvae are 300–400 µM in length and consist of about 4000 cells.
source: At 10 days post-fertilization (dpf), larvae are 300–400 µM in length and consist of about 4000 cells.
evidence: This is a specific measurement of larval size and cell number at a defined developmental stage.

claim: Larvae have a tripartite gut composed of an epithelial monolayer separated by two sphincters into a pharynx, midgut and hindgut.
source: Larvae have a tripartite gut composed of an epithelial monolayer separated by two sphincters into a pharynx, midgut and hindgut (Smith et al., 2008).
evidence: This anatomical description is supported by citation to a study on larval gut structure.

claim: Upon exposure to V. diazotrophicus, larvae exhibit a synchronous and robust set of cellular responses over a period of 24 hr.
source: Upon exposure to V. diazotrophicus, larvae exhibit a synchronous and robust set of cellular responses over a period of 24 hr (Ch Ho et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to a previous study characterizing the larval immune response.

claim: A subset of pigment cells change shape from a stellate to a rounded form, disengage from their typical positions apposed to the aboral ectoderm, and migrate to the gut epithelium upon V. diazotrophicus exposure.
source: The most notable of these is that a subset of pigment cells change shape from a stellate to a rounded form, disengage from their typical positions apposed to the aboral ectoderm, and migrate to the gut epithelium.
evidence: This cellular behavior is described and supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The gut epithelial wall thickens to constrict the midgut during V. diazotrophicus exposure, suggesting that the animals cease feeding.
source: Additionally, gut morphology is affected: the epithelial wall thickens to constrict the midgut, suggesting that the animals cease feeding.
evidence: This is an observation of morphological changes with an inference about feeding behavior.

claim: By 24 hr of V. diazotrophicus exposure, bacteria are evident within the blastocoel, where they are phagocytosed by filopodial blastocoelar cells.
source: By 24 hr, bacteria are evident within the blastocoel, where they are phagocytosed by filopodial blastocoelar cells.
evidence: This is an observation of bacterial location and cellular response at a specific time point.

claim: Early changes in gene activity are most evident within the gut epithelium within 2 hr of V. diazotrophicus exposure, which is well before bacteria penetrate the gut lumen.
source: Early changes in gene activity are most evident within the gut epithelium within 2 hr of exposure, which is well before bacteria penetrate the gut lumen.
evidence: This temporal relationship between gene expression changes and bacterial penetration is based on experimental observations.

claim: Whole transcriptome sequencing was performed on mRNA isolated from larval samples collected at 0, 6, 12 and 24 hr of exposure to V.d.
source: To investigate the transcriptional underpinnings of this response, whole transcriptome sequencing was performed on mRNA isolated from larval samples collected at 0, 6, 12 and 24 hr of exposure to V.d.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used to generate RNA-Seq data.

claim: 3238 transcripts were differentially expressed (RPKM ≥3, fold-change in expression ≥2) during the V. diazotrophicus infection time course.
source: Differentially expressed transcripts (RPKM ≥3, fold-change in expression ≥2; 3238 total transcripts) were hierarchically clustered
evidence: This is a quantitative result from RNA-Seq analysis shown in Figure 1c.

claim: 127 genes exhibit ≥3-fold changes in expression levels between 0 and 6 hr of V. diazotrophicus infection.
source: The 127 genes that exhibit ≥3-fold changes in expression levels between 0 and 6 hr of infection are shown in black.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from RNA-Seq analysis shown in Figure 1d.

claim: A small group of IL17 genes emerge as the most upregulated genes in the genome at 6 hr of V. diazotrophicus exposure.
source: From this analysis, a small group of IL17 genes emerge as the most upregulated genes in the genome (Figure 1d).
evidence: This is based on comparative analysis of gene expression changes shown in Figure 1d.

claim: SpIL17 transcripts are completely absent from transcriptomes assembled from unchallenged larvae.
source: Notably, these transcripts are completely absent from transcriptomes assembled from unchallenged (presumably immunoquiescent) larvae (Tu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on analysis of published transcriptome data from unchallenged larvae.

claim: Using BLAST searches and HMMER analyses, 34 IL17 homologs were identified in the S. purpuratus genome (v4.2).
source: Using these sequences as queries in BLAST searches, and HMMER analyses to identify IL17 domains (PF06083) in the translated genome sequence, 34 IL17 homologs were identified.
evidence: This describes the computational methods used to identify IL17 genes and the number found.

claim: 22 of the 34 identified IL17 homologs correspond to previously annotated gene models.
source: Of these, 22 correspond to previously annotated gene models (gene model numbers and coordinates are shown in Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This indicates that some IL17 genes were previously known while others are newly identified.

claim: One unannotated genomic region containing a partial IL17 domain was identified through analysis of RNA-Seq reads and experimentally confirmed using RT-PCR.
source: One of these expressed, unannotated regions contained a partial IL17 domain. Using the transcriptome data to guide the prediction of coding sequence, a second nearby exon was identified and experimentally confirmed using RT-PCR (Figure 1e).
evidence: This describes the discovery and experimental validation of a novel IL17 gene (SpIL17-4a).

claim: The S. purpuratus genome (v4.2) contains 35 homologs of IL17.
source: The S. purpuratus genome (v4.2) thus contains 35 homologs of IL17 (hereafter referred to as SpIL17).
evidence: This is the total count of IL17 genes identified through comprehensive genomic analysis.

claim: Five of the 35 SpIL17 sequences appear to be either pseudogenes or are truncated within the genome assembly.
source: Five of these sequences appear to be either pseudogenes that contain premature stop codons or frame shifts (these were verified by reference to raw unassembled trace sequence), or are truncated within the genome assembly due to sequence ambiguity.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis identifying features consistent with non-functional genes.

claim: Phylogenetic analysis indicates that the IL17 family of genes is comprised of 10 subgroups (designated SpIL17-1-10).
source: Phylogenetic analysis of the 30 remaining sequences indicates that this family of genes is comprised of 10 subgroups (designated SpIL17-1-10; Figure 2).
evidence: This classification is based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: The three closely related strongylocentrotid species have similar complements of between 30 and 47 IL17 homologs.
source: The three closely related strongylocentrotid species (S. purpuratus, S. fragilis [formerly Allocentrotus fragilis (Kober and Bernardi, 2013)], and Mesocentrotus franciscanus [formerly Strongylocentrotus franciscanus (Kober and Bernardi, 2013)]) are estimated to have similar complements of between 30 and 47 IL17 homologs.
evidence: This is based on analysis of genome sequences from multiple related species.

claim: L. variegatus, E. tribuloides, and P. miniata each have fewer IL17 genes (7-23) than strongylocentrotid species.
source: In contrast, two other sea urchins (the euechinoid Lytechinus variegatus and the cidaroid Eucidaris tribuloides) and the asteroid Patiria miniata each have fewer IL17 genes (7-23; Table 1).
evidence: This comparison of IL17 gene numbers across species is shown in Table 1.

claim: Representatives of the 10 IL17 subfamilies are present within each of the euechinoids.
source: Phylogenetic analysis of the echinoderm IL17 genes indicates that representatives of the 10 subfamilies are present within each of the euechinoids (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The E. tribuloides genome contains orthologs of most of the SpIL17 subfamilies, with the exception of groups 3, 9, and 10.
source: The more distant E. tribuloides genome also contains orthologs of most of the SpIL17 subfamilies (with the exception of groups 3, 9, and 10).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis comparing IL17 genes across echinoderm species.

claim: The conservation of IL17 families over 260 million years may reflect conserved roles within the immune response.
source: The conservation of these families over 260 million years may reflect conserved roles within the immune response.
evidence: This is an inference based on the phylogenetic conservation of IL17 subfamilies.

claim: The P. miniata IL17 sequences did not cluster with any of the echinoid sequences, with the exception of PmIL17-1.
source: Notably, the P. miniata IL17 sequences did not cluster with any of the echinoid sequences, with the exception of PmIL17-1, which is related to the EtIL17-N4 family.
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis showing divergence of asteroid IL17 sequences.

claim: The SpIL17 genes are located on nine scaffolds within the purple sea urchin genome assembly.
source: Within the purple sea urchin genome assembly, the SpIL17 genes are located on nine scaffolds (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the genomic organization of IL17 genes shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Each SpIL17 gene is encoded by one to three exons.
source: Each gene is encoded by one to three exons
evidence: This describes the gene structure of SpIL17 genes based on genomic analysis.

claim: All but five SpIL17 genes are clustered in tandem arrays of two or more genes.
source: and all but five are clustered in tandem arrays of two or more genes.
evidence: This describes the genomic organization pattern of SpIL17 genes.

claim: The genomic organization of the IL17 genes is largely conserved between S. purpuratus and L. variegatus.
source: The genomic organization of the IL17 genes is largely conserved between S. purpuratus and L. variegatus (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This comparison of genomic organization is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The SpIL17-1 genes have two exons, the first of which encodes a methionine and a single glutamate; the IL17 domain is encoded in the second exon.
source: The SpIL17-1 genes have two exons, the first of which encodes a methionine and a single glutamate; the IL17 domain is encoded in the second exon (Figure 3a).
evidence: This gene structure was confirmed by 5´ RACE PCR and RNA-Seq data.

claim: SpIL17-4a has two transcripts that initiate at exons with distinct transcription start sites but share the second and third exons.
source: SpIL17-4a has two transcripts that initiate at exons with distinct transcription start sites (TSS) but share the second and third exons.
evidence: This alternative splicing pattern was confirmed by RACE PCR and RNA-Seq analysis.

claim: The SpIL17 amino acid sequences contain eight conserved cysteine residues.
source: The SpIL17 amino acid sequences contain eight conserved cysteine residues (Figure 3c).
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment analysis shown in Figure 3c.

claim: In vertebrates, four conserved cysteine residues form disulfide bonds at the core of stereotypical cysteine-knot structures.
source: In vertebrates, four of these (highlighted in dark gray in Figure 3c) form disulfide bonds at the core of stereotypical cysteine-knot structures (Hymowitz et al., 2001).
evidence: This is established structural knowledge about IL17 proteins supported by citation.

claim: The largest SpIL17 subfamily, SpIL17-1, consists of 11 very closely related genes with 94.9% average amino acid identity.
source: The largest subfamily, SpIL17-1, consists of 11 very closely related genes (94.9% average amino acid identity; Figure 3—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: This is based on sequence identity calculations shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2a.

claim: Among SpIL17 subfamilies, proteins exhibit an average of 33.3% amino acid identity.
source: Among subfamilies, these proteins exhibit much higher diversity (an average of 33.3% amino acid identity).
evidence: This is based on sequence identity calculations across subfamilies.

claim: The six human IL17 proteins share an average 35% amino acid identity.
source: For comparison, the six human IL17 proteins share an average 35% amino acid identity (Figure 3—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: This comparison is based on sequence identity calculations for human IL17 proteins.

claim: Genes within the SpIL17-1 and SpIL17-4 subfamilies are sharply upregulated in response to microbial perturbation in the gut lumen.
source: The RNA-Seq screens of larvae exposed to V.d for 0, 6, 12, and 24 hr reveal that genes within two SpIL17 subfamilies (SpIL17-1 and −4) are sharply upregulated in response to microbial perturbation in the gut lumen (Figure 1d).
evidence: This is based on RNA-Seq data showing differential expression patterns.

claim: The SpIL17-1 genes are strongly upregulated within 2 hr of bacterial exposure, peak at 4 hr (49-fold higher than at 0 hr) and are downregulated by 8 hr.
source: In these samples, the SpIL17-1 genes are strongly upregulated within 2 hr of bacterial exposure, peak at 4 hr (49-fold higher than at 0 hr) and are downregulated by 8 hr, although expression remains higher than pre-exposure levels (Figure 4a).
evidence: This temporal expression pattern was measured by RT-qPCR as shown in Figure 4a.

claim: The 11 SpIL17-1 genes are 87.1–99.8% identical at the nucleotide level.
source: The 11 SpIL17-1 genes are 87.1–99.8% identical at the nucleotide level.
evidence: This is based on sequence comparison of the SpIL17-1 genes.

claim: Multiple SpIL17-1 genes are transcribed during infection.
source: We have isolated and sequenced SpIL17-1 transcripts from infected larvae using PCR and find that multiple genes are transcribed.
evidence: This is based on PCR amplification and sequencing of transcripts from infected larvae.

claim: Most of the SpIL17-1 genes are biallelically expressed.
source: Additionally, analysis of single-nucleotide polymorphisms within the RNA-Seq data indicates that most of the SpIL17-1 genes are biallelically expressed.
evidence: This is based on analysis of SNPs in RNA-Seq data.

claim: SpIL17-4a expression is undetectable in unexposed larvae, is activated by 2 hr of V.d. exposure, and peaks at 6 hr of exposure.
source: Like the SpIL17-1 genes, SpIL17-4a expression is undetectable in unexposed larvae, is activated by 2 hr of V.d. exposure, although its expression peaks slightly later (by 6 hr of exposure).
evidence: This temporal expression pattern was measured by RT-qPCR.

claim: SpIL17-4a is upregulated prior to SpIL17-4a´ (at 2 and 4 hr, SpIL17-4a transcripts comprise 84% and 80% of the total).
source: Results indicate that SpIL17-4a is upregulated prior to SpIL17-4a´ (at 2 and 4 hr, SpIL17-4a transcripts comprise 84% and 80% of the total; Figure 4b,c).
evidence: This is based on RT-qPCR measurements of the two transcript isoforms shown in Figure 4b,c.

claim: From 6–12 hr of V.d. exposure, expression levels are comparable for both SpIL17-4a isoforms.
source: From 6–12 hr, however, expression levels are comparable for both isoforms.
evidence: This is based on RT-qPCR measurements comparing the two transcript isoforms.

claim: The activation of the SpIL17-1 and −4 genes is one of the first transcriptional events in the larval immune response.
source: Analysis of these data reveals that the activation of the SpIL17-1 and −4 genes is one of the first transcriptional events in the larval immune response.
evidence: This is based on comparison of expression timing across multiple immune-related genes.

claim: Of the 23 genes assayed, a similarly early activation was evident only for ets4.
source: Of the 23 genes assayed, a similarly early activation was evident only for ets4 (SPU_008528, a homolog of the human Prostate-derived Ets transcription factor; PDEF [Rizzo et al., 2006]).
evidence: This is based on RT-qPCR analysis of multiple genes during the infection time course.

claim: SpIL17-1 expression was observed in the midgut and hindgut of larvae collected at 6 hr of infection (70% of larvae).
source: SpIL17-1 expression was observed in the midgut and hindgut of larvae collected at 6 hr of infection (70% of larvae; Figure 5a,c).
evidence: This spatial expression pattern was determined by WMISH as shown in Figure 5.

claim: Expression of SpIL17-4 is primarily restricted to the mid- and hindguts of larvae exposed to V.d. for 6 hr.
source: Similarly, expression of SpIL17-4 is primarily restricted to the mid- and hindguts of larvae exposed to V.d. for 6 hr, although some expression is evident at 12 hr (Figure 5b2, b3).
evidence: This spatial expression pattern was determined by WMISH as shown in Figure 5.

claim: SpIL17-1 and SpIL17-4 are largely co-expressed within the gut epithelium, but the two transcripts do not always completely overlap.
source: Fluorescent in situ hybridization using probes for both SpIL17-1 and −4 indicate that the two IL17 factors are largely co-expressed within the gut epithelium, however, the two transcripts do not always completely overlap (Figure 5d).
evidence: This co-expression pattern was determined by fluorescent in situ hybridization shown in Figure 5d.

claim: BAC-based fluorescent reporter constructs recapitulate endogenous SpIL17-1 expression.
source: Using homologous recombination, the GFP coding sequence was inserted into the coding sequence in exon 1 of the SpIL17-1d gene (shown in Figure 2a). Linearized BACs were injected into fertilized eggs, which were cultured to larval stage (10 dpf) and infected with V.d. No GFP expression was observed in larvae prior to infection (Figure 5e). By 16 hr of infection, however, fluorescent signal was evident within a few cells within the mid- and hindgut epithelium (Figure 5f,g).
evidence: This demonstrates that the BAC reporter faithfully reproduces endogenous expression patterns.

claim: The kinetics of GFP expression from the SpIL17-1 reporter are similar to that of endogenous SpIL17-1 expression.
source: RT-qPCR quantitation of GFP transcript levels normalized to incorporated transgene copy number confirms that the kinetics of GFP expression are similar to that of endogenous SpIL17-1 expression, with a sharp increase in expression by 8 hr that is attenuated at 24 hr of infection (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on RT-qPCR measurements of GFP transcript levels shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The SpIL17-4 BAC reporter construct recapitulates endogenous SpIL17-4 expression.
source: For this gene, the GFP coding sequence was inserted into the second exon, which is common to both transcripts (see Figure 2b) and analyzed as above. This reporter construct also recapitulates endogenous SpIL17-4 expression. No fluorescence was observed in uninfected larvae, but by 24 hr of infection, GFP was evident in midgut epithelial cells (Figure 4h,i)
evidence: This demonstrates that the BAC reporter faithfully reproduces endogenous expression patterns.

claim: The SpIL17-1 and −4 genes are expressed exclusively in the epithelial cells of the larval mid- and hindgut.
source: Together, these data confirm that the SpIL17-1 and −4 genes are expressed exclusively in the epithelial cells of the larval mid- and hindgut
evidence: This conclusion is based on WMISH and BAC reporter data showing gut epithelial expression.

claim: Expression of SpIL17-1 and −4 genes is tightly regulated and dependent upon bacterial challenge.
source: and that expression of these genes is tightly regulated and dependent upon bacterial challenge.
evidence: This is based on the absence of expression in unchallenged larvae and rapid induction upon bacterial exposure.

claim: Genes within the SpIL17-9 subfamily were expressed at low levels in coelomocytes at 12 hr after immune challenge.
source: Analysis of the RNA-Seq data indicated that while SpIL17 expression was not detected in the gut tissue, genes within a third subfamily, SpIL17-9, were expressed at low levels in coelomocytes at 12 hr after challenge.
evidence: This is based on analysis of RNA-Seq data from adult immune cells.

claim: The SpIL17-9 genes are strongly upregulated within 3 hr of V. diazotrophicus injection in adult coelomocytes.
source: RT-qPCR analysis indicates that the SpIL17-9 genes are strongly upregulated within 3 hr of infection in both animals injected with bacteria (red bars; Figure 6a).
evidence: This temporal expression pattern was measured by RT-qPCR as shown in Figure 6.

claim: SpIL17-9 expression peaks at 6 hr after V. diazotrophicus injection in adult coelomocytes.
source: Expression peaks at 6 hr, and then returns to lower levels.
evidence: This is based on RT-qPCR measurements of SpIL17-9 expression over time.

claim: SpIL17-9 expression precedes expression of the 185/333 genes in adult coelomocytes.
source: This timing precedes expression of the 185/333 genes, which are slightly upregulated at 3 hr of infection, but exhibit high levels of expression by 9 hr (Figure 6b).
evidence: This temporal relationship is based on RT-qPCR measurements shown in Figure 6.

claim: There is no evidence of expression of SpIL17-9 genes in larvae responding to V.d. exposure.
source: We found no evidence of expression of SpIL17-9 genes in larvae responding to V.d. exposure
evidence: This is based on the absence of SpIL17-9 transcripts in larval RNA-Seq and RT-qPCR data.

claim: SpIL17-1 or −4 expression was never evident in adult coelomocytes.
source: and SpIL17-1 or −4 expression was never evident in the adult coelomocytes.
evidence: This is based on the absence of SpIL17-1 and -4 transcripts in adult coelomocyte RNA-Seq and RT-qPCR data.

claim: Genes within at least three of the SpIL17 subfamilies are expressed in the course of the sea urchin immune response and the subfamilies are deployed in distinct tissues during different life stages.
source: Together, these data indicate that genes within at least three of the SpIL17 subfamilies are expressed in the course of the sea urchin immune response and that the subfamilies are deployed in distinct tissues during the different life stages
evidence: This is a synthesis of expression data from larvae and adults showing tissue- and stage-specific expression.

claim: Two sea urchin genes encode SEFIR domains (SpIL17R1 and SpIL17R2).
source: We find that two sea urchin genes encode SEFIR domains (SpIL17R1 and SpIL17R2; Figure 7; Figure 7—figure supplement 1a,b).
evidence: This is based on domain prediction analysis using HMMER.

claim: Each SpIL17 receptor gene encodes a signal sequence, a long putative extracellular region, a transmembrane region, and a cytoplasmic SEFIR domain.
source: Each of these genes encodes a signal sequence, a long putative extracellular region (535 or 662 amino acids), a transmembrane region, and a cytoplasmic SEFIR domain.
evidence: This protein structure was determined by sequence analysis and domain prediction.

claim: A TIR-like loop (TILL) sequence is present in SpIL17R1 directly C-terminal to the SEFIR domain but is absent in SpIL17R2.
source: Additionally, phylogenetic analysis of the sea urchin SEFIR domains supports homology with IL17 receptors in other species (Figure 7—figure supplement 1). We have confirmed these sequences by amplifying the receptors using PCR and sequencing. A TIR-like loop (TILL) sequence is present in SpIL17R1 directly C-terminal to the SEFIR domain but is absent in SpIL17R2 (Figure 7).
evidence: This structural difference was identified through sequence analysis and confirmed by PCR and sequencing.

claim: SpIL17R1 is encoded in 17 exons.
source: SpIL17R1 is encoded in 17 exons (Figure 7—figure supplement 3a).
evidence: This gene structure was determined by genomic and transcriptomic analysis.

claim: Exon 16 of SpIL17R1 is alternatively spliced and is absent from some transcripts.
source: Exon 16, which encodes the sequence between the transmembrane region and the SEIFR domain is alternatively spliced and is absent from some transcripts.
evidence: This alternative splicing was identified through analysis of transcript sequences.

claim: SpIL17R2 is expressed in 16 exons; the last exon encodes the SEFIR domain.
source: Similarly, SpIL17R2 is expressed in 16 exons; the last exon encodes the SEFIR domain (Figure 7—figure supplement 3a).
evidence: This gene structure was determined by genomic and transcriptomic analysis.

claim: No homolog of Act1 was identified in any of the echinoderm genomes.
source: Despite extensive searches, we were not able to identify a homolog of Act1 (the SEFIR domain-containing adaptor molecule for the IL17 receptor in vertebrates [Qian et al., 2007]) in any of the echinoderm genomes.
evidence: This is based on comprehensive searches of echinoderm genome sequences.

claim: The L. variegatus genome contains two IL17 receptors and lacks an Act1 homolog.
source: Similarly, the L. variegatus genome contains two IL17 receptors and lacks an Act1 homolog (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the L. variegatus genome sequence.

claim: The sea urchin IL17 receptors may signal through an Act1-independent mechanism.
source: This suggests that the sea urchin IL17 receptors signal through an Act1-independent mechanism.
evidence: This is an inference based on the absence of Act1 homologs in echinoderm genomes.

claim: Treatment with the SpIL17R1 splice-blocking MASO produces incorrectly spliced SpIL17R1 transcripts with a frame shift and premature stop codon.
source: Analysis of these sequences indicates that treatment with the MASOS produces incorrectly spliced SpIL17R1 transcripts, in which an alternative donor site within exon 14 is spliced directly to exon 16, resulting in a frame shift and premature stop codon.
evidence: This was confirmed by amplifying and sequencing SpIL17R1 transcripts from MASO-treated larvae.

claim: The truncated SpIL17R1 protein produced by MASO treatment does not encode a transmembrane domain.
source: The subsequently translated protein does not encode a transmembrane domain (Figure 7a).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the predicted protein sequence from the mis-spliced transcript.

claim: Perturbation of IL17 signaling during larval immune challenge does not significantly affect pigment cell migration.
source: Perturbation of IL17 signaling during the larval immune challenge does not significantly affect pigment cell migration (Figure 7—figure supplement 3h)
evidence: This was assessed by counting migratory pigment cells in MASO-treated larvae shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3h.

claim: Perturbation of IL17 signaling affects the message prevalence of several genes including SpIL17-4, tnfaip3, soul1, nfkbiz, cebpα, and cebpγ.
source: however, it does affect the message prevalence of several genes that were chosen as candidate response genes from the timing of their upregulation (Figure 7b, Figure 7—figure supplement 4). Notably, this includes SpIL17-4, which is upregulated relative to uninfected larvae, but at 2–5-fold lower levels than in larvae injected with control MASO. This decreased expression, in addition to the fact that SpIL17-1 expression consistently lags that of peak SpIL17-4 (Figure 4d) suggests that the SpIL17-1 signaling may be involved in upregulating SpIL17-4. Additionally, transcript levels of tnfaip3, soul1, nfkbiz, cebpα, and cebpγ are reduced in larvae exposed to the SpIL17R1 MASOs compared to control MASO (Figure 7b, Figure 7—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This was measured by RT-qPCR comparing gene expression in MASO-treated vs. control larvae.

claim: SpIL17-1 signaling may be involved in upregulating SpIL17-4.
source: This decreased expression, in addition to the fact that SpIL17-1 expression consistently lags that of peak SpIL17-4 (Figure 4d) suggests that the SpIL17-1 signaling may be involved in upregulating SpIL17-4.
evidence: This is inferred from the reduced SpIL17-4 expression when IL17R1 is perturbed and the temporal relationship between SpIL17-1 and SpIL17-4 expression.

claim: Epithelial expression of IL17 signaling is an ancient and central element of the gut associated immune response.
source: These findings reveal that epithelial IL17 signaling is an ancient and central element of the gut associated immune response.
evidence: This is a synthesis conclusion based on the expression data showing gut epithelial IL17 expression in sea urchins and comparison to mammalian systems.

claim: The conservation of the IL-17 subfamilies may indicate functional compartmentalization for these genes within the echinoderm immune response.
source: The conservation of the IL-17 subfamilies may indicate functional compartmentalization for these genes within the echinoderm immune response.
evidence: This is an inference based on the phylogenetic conservation and differential expression patterns of IL17 subfamilies.

claim: IL17C is produced by the gut epithelium where it acts in an autocrine manner to activate expression of genes involved in the innate immune response.
source: IL17C is produced by the gut epithelium where it acts in an autocrine manner to activate expression of genes involved in the innate immune response, including proinflammatory cytokines and antimicrobial peptides (Song et al., 2011; Ramirez-Carrozzi et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge about mammalian IL17C function supported by citations.

claim: IL17C plays a role in maintaining intestinal barrier integrity by regulating the expression of occludin.
source: IL17C plays a role in maintaining intestinal barrier integrity by regulating the expression of occludin, a tight junction protein in colonic epithelial cells (Reynolds et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge about IL17C function supported by citation.

claim: In the lamprey, five IL17 homologs are differentially expressed on skin, kidney, intestine and gills, as well as VLRA+, VLRB+ and VLRC+ lymphocytes.
source: In the lamprey, five IL17 homologs are differentially expressed on skin, kidney, intestine and gills, as well as VLRA+, VLRB+ and VLRC+ lymphocytes (Han et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited information about IL17 expression in lamprey.

claim: Ciona intestinalis upregulates three homologs of IL17 in the pharynx and in immune cells in response to LPS challenge.
source: Ciona intestinalis upregulates three homologs of IL17 in the pharynx and in immune cells in response to LPS challenge (Vizzini et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited information about IL17 expression in Ciona.

claim: In the oyster, the single IL17 homolog is expressed by circulating hemocytes in response to infection.
source: In the oyster, which is the only protostome in which the IL17 response has been characterized, the single IL17 homolog is expressed by circulating hemocytes in response to infection (Roberts et al., 2008).
evidence: This is cited information about IL17 expression in oyster.

claim: In the sea urchin larva, SpIL17 expression is restricted to gut epithelial cells, with no evidence of expression in mesodermally derived immune cells in response to V.d. challenge.
source: In the work presented here, we show that in the sea urchin larva, SpIL17 expression is restricted to gut epithelial cells, with no evidence of expression in mesodermally derived immune cells in response to V.d. challenge.
evidence: This is based on WMISH and BAC reporter data showing exclusive gut epithelial expression.

claim: The role of IL17 in modulating mucosal immunity is an ancient and fundamental component of immunity.
source: This function is potentially homologous to the mammalian epithelial expression and suggests that the role of IL17 in modulating mucosal immunity is an ancient and fundamental component of immunity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the conservation of epithelial IL17 expression between sea urchins and mammals.

claim: The gut epithelium is a primary site of SpIL17R1 expression.
source: In situ hybridization indicates that the gut epithelium is a primary site of SpIL17R1 expression (Figure 7—figure supplement 3e).
evidence: This spatial expression pattern was determined by WMISH shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3e.

claim: SpIL17R1 is also expressed in gcm+ pigment cells.
source: Analysis of cell-specific transcriptome data from larvae indicates that this receptor is also expressed in gcm+ pigment cells (Barsi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is based on analysis of published cell-specific transcriptome data.

claim: SpIL17R1 contains conserved tyrosine residues (444 and 454) that may mediate STAT5 recruitment.
source: One potential mechanism identified in mammals is the direct activation of STAT5 that occurs in vertebrate IL17RB signaling (Wu et al., 2015). The recruitment of STAT5 depends on phosphorylation of specific tyrosine residues within the IL17RB cytoplasmic region. Specifically, STAT5 recruitment is mediated by tyrosine residues 444 and 454. These residues are both conserved in the SpIL17-R1 sequence.
evidence: This is based on sequence comparison identifying conserved tyrosine residues that function in STAT5 recruitment in mammals.

claim: The IL17R1 is expressed in the gut epithelial cells consistent with the possibility that neighboring cells in the epithelium could communicate using the IL17-1 signal.
source: Several observations are consistent with feedback in the larval gut epithelial system. The IL17R1 is expressed in the gut epithelial cells consistent with the possibility that neighboring cells in the epithelium could communicate using the IL17-1 signal.
evidence: This is an inference based on the co-expression of IL17-1 and IL17R1 in gut epithelial cells.

claim: Reduction of IL17-4 expression in IL17R1 MASO perturbed embryos supports a causal linkage between IL17-1 activation and later IL17-4 expression.
source: Reduction of IL17-4 expression in IL17R1 MASO perturbed embryos supports a causal linkage between IL17-1 activation and later IL17-4 expression.
evidence: This is based on experimental data showing reduced IL17-4 expression when IL17R1 is perturbed.

claim: V. diazotrophicus was first isolated from the gastrointestinal tract of the congeneric green sea urchin, S. droebachiensis.
source: This marine bacterium was first isolated from the gastrointestinal tract of the congeneric green sea urchin, S. droebachiensis (Guerinot et al., 1982).
evidence: This is cited information about the origin of V. diazotrophicus.

claim: Other Vibrio species have been implicated as causative disease agents in several adult sea urchins species.
source: Other Vibrio species have been implicated as causative disease agents in several adult sea urchins species (Becker et al., 2008).
evidence: This is cited information about Vibrio as a pathogen in sea urchins.

claim: SpIL17R1 expression is not evident at 12 hpf, but increases slowly to prism larval stage (84 hpf).
source: qPCR indicates that SpIL17R1 expression is not evident at 12 hpf, but increases slowly to prism larval stage (84 hpf).
evidence: This developmental expression pattern was measured by qPCR.

claim: SpIL17R2 is upregulated at 24 hpf, peaks at 48 hpf, and then returns to low levels into the larval stage.
source: SpIL17R2 is upregulated at 24 hpf, peaks at 48 hpf, and then returns to low levels into the larval stage (Figure 7—figure supplement 3c).
evidence: This developmental expression pattern was measured by qPCR shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3c.

claim: In larvae, spIL17R1 is gradually downregulated during infection.
source: In larvae, spIL17R1 is gradually downregulated during infection
evidence: This expression pattern during infection was measured by qPCR.

claim: SpIL17R2 expression is mostly constant but exhibits a small peak at 2 hr of infection and then again at 24 hr.
source: whereas SpIL17R2 expression is mostly constant but exhibits a small peak at 2 hr of infection and then again at 24 hr (Figure 7—figure supplement 3d,f).
evidence: This expression pattern during infection was measured by qPCR shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3d,f.

claim: Low expression of spIL17-R1 is evident in adult gut and testes.
source: Results indicate that low expression of spIL17-R1 is evident in adult gut and testes.
evidence: This is based on analysis of publicly available RNA-Seq data from adult tissues.

claim: The spIL17r2 transcript was not clearly present in any of the adult tissues assayed.
source: The spIL17r2 transcript was not clearly present in any of the adult tissues assayed.
evidence: This is based on analysis of publicly available RNA-Seq data from adult tissues.
